1947, October 4.
Dr. J. P. Young
Page 3.
But you dear Doctor; while in quite a number of ways you have been doing good - have been an asset and a credit to the Community at least as far as the general public sees. You have used the talents God has lent you to a great extent in a creditable manner. Has not God bles'd you too, and temporarily at least filled your heart with grateful appreciation for the ability to do for Him and for humanity? But are you going to drift on, and into eternity satisfied with the natural "rick you get out of it"? - and the temporal advantages, including in this latter the shadowy credit of an unthinking public? I am asking - addressing - these questions as to a brother who can draw conclusions; as to one who, in the sight of Heaven can not plead ignorance. Are you going to continue till too late, to tacitly defy the Church of the Living God - doping your conscience with the poison of modern atheism, the climax of intellectual and moral in- sanity, that you can get along without the Church and her sacraments and consequently without God?
Get along without the Church? A peacemaker without humbly confessing one's own sins? ! "Charity begins at home". Peace is an outstanding characteristic of charity. They accompany eachother and must begin, if really genuine, between God and the individual soul. ... "without me you can do nothing." "He that is not with me is against me and he that gatherith not with me, scattereth." "He that heareth you heareth me ... "
If the withdrawal of grace is the first punishment on sin, which means the flight of the Holy Spirit from the soul guilty of sin and if peace is outstandingly a gift of the Holy Spriit, and furthermore, if one of the parents of a family virtully defy the divinely installed and established representative of peace, then Doctor; can any thinker aquainted with the case be surprised at the scandallous want of peace in such a parents home? -- and of course, that every immediate member of the family be upset is quite to be expected. Fo positive faith fostered or appreciated, or moral obligations for a rational creature? Is it not as selfunderstood, Doctor; at least with philosophers, that all these necessarily go together - reason, moral obligation, appreciation, religion?
